a: the second year of King Darius
p: Haggai dates every message. The first is 29 August 520 BC by the usual conversion.
b: Darius I took the Persian throne in 522 BC and spent his first two years putting down revolts in Babylon, Elam, Media and elsewhere; his own Behistun inscription lists them. Counted as Persian and Babylonian scribes counted, his second year began in the spring of 520. The first of Haggai's dates, the first day of the sixth month, converts to 29 August 520 BC (the figures in this book use the usual conversion to the Julian calendar). Ezra says the Temple work "stayed stopped until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia" (Ezra 4:24). The book gives six dates in all (1:1, 15; 2:1, 10, 18, 20), on four different days, and they run from August to December of one year, about 66 years after Solomon's Temple was burned in 586 BC.

a: the word of the LORD came
t: The LORD, and a prophet's word
p: The divine name is written "the LORD"; "the word of the LORD came" opens each of the book's messages.
b: The Hebrew has the four letters YHWH, the personal name of Israel's God, which most English Bibles print as "the LORD" in capitals. "God" (Elohim) is the common word, and the book uses both (1:12, 14). "The word of the LORD came" is the standard opening of a prophet's message. Haggai uses it five times (1:1, 3; 2:1, 10, 20), with "through" (literally "by the hand of," beyad) at 1:1, 3 and 2:1, and "to" at 2:10 and 2:20. The Plain keeps that difference. The Murabba'at scroll of the Twelve seems to read "to" even at 2:1 (see the variant there).

p: Haggai is named only here and in Ezra; the book speaks of him in the third person.
b: The name Chaggai looks like it comes from chag, "festival" (perhaps "born on a feast day"); nothing more is known of his family. Outside this book he appears only in Ezra, which pairs him with Zechariah son of Iddo and says they prophesied to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem in the name of Israel's God (Ezra 5:1; Ezra 6:14). The book never says "I": the prophet is "Haggai the prophet" or "the LORD's messenger" (1:13), so the words were put in order by someone other than Haggai, who may be a disciple, a scribe or a later editor (see the book's introduction). His age is unknown. Because he asks who is left that saw the first Temple (2:3), some have guessed he did himself; the text does not say so. The Talmud counts Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi as the last prophets, after whom the Holy Spirit left Israel (Bavli Yoma 9b).

a: Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah
p: Zerubbabel is a grandson of King Jehoiachin, the last Davidic king to reign in Jerusalem before the exile, and the Persians' governor.
b: Pechah ("governor") is the Persian-era title for the head of a province; Ezra uses the same word for Tattenai, governor of Beyond the River (Ezra 5:3). Judah (Hebrew Yehud) was a small district inside that larger region. Zerubbabel's name is Babylonian (Zer-Babili, "offspring of Babylon"). Ezra 3:2 and Matthew 1:12 call him son of Shealtiel, and Shealtiel was a son of King Jehoiachin (Jeconiah), taken to Babylon in 597 BC (1 Chronicles 3:17). First Chronicles 3:19 names Pedaiah, Shealtiel's brother, as his father: a levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5-6) or a difference between family records are the usual explanations. Sheshbazzar, "prince of Judah," led the first return (Ezra 1:8); whether he and Zerubbabel are the same man is debated.

a: Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest
p: Haggai spells the high priest's name in full; Ezra shortens it to Jeshua son of Jozadak.
b: The Hebrew is Yehoshua', "Joshua," the same name as Moses' helper. Ezra and Nehemiah, written later, use the shortened Yeshua', which this site's Plain spells "Jeshua" (Ezra 3:2; Nehemiah 12:1), and they spell his father "Jozadak." Haggai (and Zechariah) have the full forms, and the Plain follows them. Jehozadak is the form in 1 Chronicles 6:15, which says he went into exile when the LORD drove Judah and Jerusalem out through Nebuchadnezzar. His own father, Seraiah, was the chief priest executed at Riblah in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:18-21). So Joshua is a priest born or raised in exile, now the head of the priesthood. "The high priest" is literally "the great priest" (hakkohen haggadol).

p: A title of the LORD as commander of heavenly and earthly forces; it appears 14 times in these 38 verses.
b: YHWH tseva'ot. "Armies" may mean Israel's armies, the angels or the stars; scholars differ, and the older English "LORD of hosts" keeps the question open. The Plain's "Armies" follows the site's term for the title in every book. In Haggai the title is almost a signature: it is the voice that asks for wood and stones from a poor community and promises to shake nations. The Greek Septuagint renders it Kyrios Pantokrator ("Lord Almighty"), and many English Bibles follow that, which makes the title sound only like a title of power. Haggai ties it to the Temple: the LORD of Armies, whose are the silver and the gold (2:8), asks for a house.

p: The Hebrew is ha'am hazzeh, not "my people": a cool phrase, used here and in 2:14.
b: God does not say "my people" ('ammi) but "this people" (ha'am hazzeh), the way he speaks to Isaiah about a people who will not hear (Isaiah 6:9; Isaiah 8:6). It can be plain distance, a rebuke, or only the speaker's way of reporting what "this people" are saying. Haggai uses the phrase again at 2:14, where it is strongest. Between the two, once the leaders and the remnant obey (1:12-14), the book speaks of "the people" and "the remnant of the people," and the LORD says "I am with you" (1:13). The change of words inside the book is part of its argument: this people becomes the remnant when it listens.

p: The text quotes the excuse but does not say why the people made it. Commentators offer several reasons.
b: The Hebrew is a clipped quotation: "Not time to come, time of the LORD's house to be rebuilt." Reasons proposed: (1) The seventy years of Jeremiah 25:11-12 and 29:10, counted from the Temple's burning in 586 BC, would end in 516, so the work would be early (a view in several commentaries, for example Petersen and Meyers and Meyers). (2) Hard times and the neighbors' opposition (Ezra 4:4-5, 24). (3) Politics: Darius's first years were unstable, and a rebuilt Temple might look like rebellion. (4) The poor harvests (1:6, 10-11) left no money. Rashi on 1:2 gives a fifth: because their enemies had stopped them the first time, the people thought God would not fulfill what he had said. The text only says what the people said; God answers by pointing to their own houses (1:4). The doubled "time" in the Hebrew is shorter in the Greek (see the variant).

p: The Hebrew sefunim means "covered": wood-lined rooms, a mark of money. The Plain avoids "paneled."
b: Sefunim is "covered" (also "lined" or "roofed"). It is used of Solomon's Temple and palace walls covered with cedar (1 Kings 6:9; 1 Kings 7:3, 7) and of the king who builds himself "a roomy house" with windows cut in and cedar over it (Jeremiah 22:14). Haggai's phrase therefore says that the people's own homes are finished to a standard the kings once kept for God's house. Whether every Judean had wooden ceilings is doubtful, and the line may be a sharp exaggeration aimed at the leaders and better-off families. Rashi explains "covered" as covered with boards of cedar. "You, yes you" ('attem) is stressed: the pronoun stands by itself in Hebrew.

p: One Hebrew sound, chareb and choreb, links the ruined house to the drought.
b: The house is chareb, "desolate, dry waste" (1:4, 9). In 1:11 the LORD summons a choreb, "drought." The consonants are the same, and the Greek's "sword" in 1:11 (see the variant) reads the same consonants again as chereb. Hebrew listeners would have heard one sound run through the speech: a desolate house, a drought on the land. English cannot keep the single sound, so the Plain uses "desolate" for the house and "drought" for the weather, and the note points out the link. Nehemiah uses the same root of Jerusalem in ruins (Nehemiah 2:17).

p: The Hebrew simu levavkhem 'al darkeikhem means "set your heart on your ways." It returns at 1:7 and 2:15, 18.
b: Literally "set your heart upon your ways." In Hebrew the "heart" is the mind: to set it on something is to think it through. The usual English is "consider your ways" (the KJV, from the old sense of "think over"). The Plain uses the same words each time the formula appears (1:5, 7; 2:15, 18), so the reader sees it as the book's refrain. In 1:5 and 1:7 the thing to examine is "your ways," how they have been living and what has come of it; in 2:15 and 2:18 the object is a time and its results. The call is neither "feel bad" nor "try harder": it is "look at the pattern of these years and ask why."

a: You have sown much, but you bring in little
p: Haggai's list of failed harvests reuses the covenant curse of Deuteronomy 28.
b: The pattern "sow much, harvest little; eat, but not be full" is the covenant curse for disobedience: "You will sow plenty of seed in the field and harvest little" (Deuteronomy 28:38). Micah 6:14-15 and Zephaniah 1:13 describe the same things, eating that does not satisfy and houses and vineyards that others enjoy. Haggai takes the curse and points it at a specific cause: the unbuilt house. The same chain returns at 2:16-17, and the first sign of a turn is the promised blessing of 2:19. Whether the poor harvests of these years were an ordinary famine or a special judgment, the prophet reads them as the covenant working, and he is not alone in the Twelve (Amos 4:6-9).

a: never to the point of being drunk
p: "Drunk" here marks the limit of plenty, not a recommendation.
b: The Hebrew shakar means "to be drunk." The line is about abundance cut off: there is not enough to drink even to a full cup, which in the language of plenty meant drinking one's fill (Genesis 43:34; Song of Songs 5:1). It does not praise drunkenness, which the Bible elsewhere condemns (Proverbs 20:1; Ephesians 5:18). Some translations soften it to "never have enough." The Plain keeps the Hebrew word and the note explains. Eating, drinking, clothing and wages are four needs; the fifth, shelter, is the one the people have already looked after (1:4).

a: a bag with holes poked in it
p: Wages were silver weighed out and carried in a bag; coined money was only beginning.
b: A tserur is a bag or bundle for silver (Genesis 42:35; Proverbs 7:20). In 520 BC most payment was silver by weight, not coins: the gold daric of the Persian kings, usually credited to Darius I, was just coming into use. A bag "pierced through" (naqub) is a plain image of money that drains away as fast as it comes in. The book does not say what caused the shortages. The point of the image is the one the prophet states next: the problem is not income but where the effort goes.

p: What the builders lacked was timber and the will to cut it. Whether a foundation already stood is debated (see 2:18).
b: The Hebrew says "go up to the hill" (hahar), which can mean the hill country around Jerusalem. The work is cutting and hauling timber for beams and roof. Cedar from Lebanon had been ordered through the Sidonians in the first return (Ezra 3:7), and Cyrus's decree called for a course of new timber with every three courses of large stones (Ezra 6:3-4). Nothing in Haggai says he is asking for cedar; local wood from the hills is what he names. The command is small and plain: this is a job people could start the next morning, and 1:14-15 says they did, 23 days later.

a: I will be pleased with it
p: Ratsah is the word for the LORD accepting an offering. The Plain keeps the sacrificial sense.
b: Ratsah is to be pleased with, to accept favorably; it is the verb for the LORD accepting an offering (Leviticus 1:4, where the offering is "accepted"). Here the LORD is pleased with a house, as if the building were itself an offering. The next verb, "I will be honored" ('ekkavdah, from kavod, "glory"), is the verb form of the noun the book uses for the "first glory" and "last glory" (2:3, 9). The Hebrew puts both verbs in a form that expresses purpose ("so that I may be pleased... and honored"), which the Plain softens into "Then" to keep the sentence plain.
orig: וְאֶרְצֶה־בּוֹ (ve'ertseh-bo), 'and I will be pleased with it'

p: The LORD breathes on the harvest the way a wind blows on grass: it is gone.
b: The verb nafach is to blow or puff, and the LORD says he "blew on it," on what they brought in. Isaiah 40:7 has the same picture with a different verb: the LORD's breath on grass, and it withers. The grain is not stolen; it simply dwindles after it comes in. The Greek puts it plainly: "I blew them away." The Hebrew also makes it close and personal: the God who stirs the spirit in 1:14 blows on the harvest in 1:9. The Plain keeps the literal phrase and leaves the sense to the context.
orig: וְנָפַחְתִּי בוֹ (venafachti vo), 'and I blew on it'

p: The Hebrew says only "the house," the same word as the Temple in 1:8. Most read it as the people's own homes.
b: In 1:8 "the house" is the LORD's. In 1:9 "you brought it to the house" (habbayit) has no pronoun. Most commentators take it as the household's home: they brought the harvest in, and it shrank. A few hear a play on the double use of "house" in the verse, and a few think of the Temple itself. The readings share one moral, and the verse ends by setting "my house" against "his own house." The Plain's "the house" keeps the ambiguity, and the context leans toward "home."

p: The speech ties lean harvests to an unbuilt house. It is not a rule for all giving or all hardship.
b: Haggai 1 is sometimes quoted to say that giving to a church brings wealth, or that hardship proves neglected duty. The Hebrew does not say that. The speech has a specific audience (a small community in one province), a specific cause (an unbuilt Temple that the covenant made central), and a specific covenant background (Deuteronomy 28 and Leviticus 26). Elsewhere the Bible lets the righteous suffer: Job's friends are wrong to say so (Job 42:7-8), and Jesus denies that a tower's fall or a blind man's birth proves someone's sin (Luke 13:4; John 9:3). Even in Haggai the prophet asks the hearers to look at their own ways (1:5, 7), not at someone else's poverty. The blessing of 2:19 follows obedience; it is not a payment for a gift.

p: Withheld dew and rain are the covenant curse of Deuteronomy and the prayer of Solomon.
b: Dew is the summer moisture on which crops live between the spring and autumn rains. "The LORD will shut up the sky, and there will be no rain" is the curse for turning to other gods (Deuteronomy 11:17). Solomon's Temple prayer lists such a drought as a time to pray toward the Temple (1 Kings 8:35-36). Haggai's point is bitter: the Temple that would be the place to pray for rain is the building they have not built. The Hebrew phrase "over you" ('alekhem) can also mean "because of you"; the Plain uses "over you" and the cause is in 1:9. The Greek is shorter and has no "you" (see the variant).

p: The LORD "calls" (qara') a drought as one calls a servant. Compare the famine in 2 Kings 8:1.
b: The verb qara' is "call" or "summon," and the object is something that comes at the LORD's word: "The LORD has summoned a famine" (2 Kings 8:1). Haggai's list is the same in kind: drought, then every product of the land (grain, wine, oil), then people, livestock and "all that hands labor for." The Hebrew list runs from the highest to the smallest, from land and hills to the work of the hand. The word for "drought" (choreb) puns on "desolate" (see 1:4).

a: the grain, the new wine and the fresh oil
p: The three products of the land are a fixed trio in Deuteronomy, and the site's Plain keeps the same English for them.
b: Dagan, tirosh, yitshar: grain, new wine, fresh oil. They are the three crops of the covenant's promised blessing (Deuteronomy 7:13; Deuteronomy 11:14) and the three that fail in Joel 1:10 ("the grain is wrecked, the new wine has gone dry, and the fresh oil has withered"). Haggai names the full trio so that every harvest is covered, and 2:12 will use two of them, wine and oil, in the priestly question. The first fruits and tithes of this trio were the Temple's income (Deuteronomy 12:17; Numbers 18:12), so a failed harvest also starved the house they were not building.

a: all the remnant of the people
p: She'erit ha'am means those who are left: here, mainly the community of returned exiles.
b: She'erit is "what is left over," and the site's Plain renders it "remnant" everywhere. Haggai uses it at 1:12, 14 and 2:2. The word comes with weight from earlier prophets (Isaiah 10:20-22; Jeremiah 23:3), where the remnant is the small group that survives judgment and is the seed of renewal. Who exactly is meant is debated: the returned exiles who came under Cyrus and Darius (Ezra 1-2; the most common view, Meyers, Petersen, Kessler), the whole population of Judah, or those who were faithful. Haggai's use is plain: the remnant is the community of his own day, small and poor, and its first act is to listen.

a: listened to the voice of the LORD their God
p: To "listen to the voice" is to obey; the leaders treat Haggai's words as the LORD's voice.
b: In Hebrew "listen to the voice of" (shama' beqol) means to heed and obey; it is the standard covenant phrase (Deuteronomy 11:13; Exodus 19:5). Verse 12 makes two things equal: "the voice of the LORD their God" and "the words of Haggai the prophet," because the LORD had sent him. The people do what the earlier generation did not do, for the same prophetic word (Jeremiah 7:23-26). Their fear is "before the LORD," not of Haggai: it is the awe the Bible calls the beginning of wisdom, shown by action. First the leaders listen, then all the remnant; their obedience sets the pattern that 1:14 completes.

p: Mal'ak is "messenger." Haggai is, as far as I know, the only prophet given this exact title.
b: The word mal'ak is "messenger" or "angel," and the second word, mal'akut ("message"), appears only here in the Bible. The wordplay is "the messenger of the LORD, with the message of the LORD." Prophets are elsewhere called messengers (Isaiah 44:26; 2 Chronicles 36:15-16; Malachi 3:1 is "my messenger" and is the origin of the name Malachi), and Haggai is, as far as I know, the only prophet in the Hebrew Bible given the title "messenger of the LORD" outright (Malachi 2:7 uses it of a priest); I have not found a commentary that says so. The Greek reads "the angel of the Lord among the angels of the Lord," and the Greek wording could be read to make Haggai a heavenly being (see the variant). Rashi on 1:13 reads the Hebrew the other way: Haggai spoke in the messengership of the Omnipresent. The Plain uses "messenger," which fits both the Hebrew and the commissioned-envoy sense.
orig: מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה בְּמַלְאֲכוּת יְהוָה (mal'akh YHWH bemal'akhut YHWH)

p: The shortest message in the book is two Hebrew words, and it is the promise given to Moses, Joshua and Isaiah.
b: 'Ani 'ittekhem, "I am with you," is the whole message of 1:13, and it returns at 2:4. It is the promise at the burning bush (Exodus 3:12), to Joshua (Joshua 1:9) and in Isaiah's comfort (Isaiah 41:10). It also echoes the name of the child "God with us" (Isaiah 7:14) and is repeated by Jesus at the end of Matthew (Matthew 28:20). Here it works as the pivot of chapter 1: before it, a rebuke and a drought; after it, the LORD stirs their spirit to work. The promise comes after the people have obeyed (1:12), not before; the Hebrew gives no condition, only the fact.
orig: אֲנִי אִתְּכֶם (ani ittekhem), 'I am with you'

p: Ne'um YHWH is a noun, "an utterance of the LORD." It appears 12 times in the book.
b: Ne'um means "utterance," a solemn pronouncement, and ne'um YHWH is "the LORD declares." Prophets use it to mark God's own words, often at the end of a clause. Haggai has it 12 times in 38 verses, usually at the end of a sentence and often twice in one verse (2:4, 23). The Plain distinguishes it from 'amar YHWH, "says the LORD" (1:8; 2:7, 9), which is a plainer verb. Together with "The LORD of Armies says this," the formulas keep telling the hearer that this is not Haggai's opinion but the LORD's word through him.

p: The verb he'ir is the same one the site's Ezra uses of Cyrus and the first returnees.
b: The LORD "roused the spirit" of Cyrus (Ezra 1:1) and of "all those whose spirit God had roused" to go up from Babylon (Ezra 1:5). Here the same verb applies to Zerubbabel, Joshua and the remnant. Its older use is of the LORD rousing a king of Assyria against Israel (1 Chronicles 5:26). The point is plain: God's rousing the spirit works through a human will, and the result in 1:14 is that they "came" and "did the work." The text does not say how the spirit was roused: through Haggai's words, through the harvest, or in ways no one saw. Zechariah, working at the same time, gives the same credit to God's spirit (Zechariah 4:6).

a: They came and did the work
p: The work was clearing, cutting and building. Whether a foundation already stood is debated (see 2:18).
b: Ezra 5:2 says Zerubbabel and Jeshua "got up and began to build God's house in Jerusalem," with the prophets helping. The governor of Beyond the River, Tattenai, came to ask who had authorized it (Ezra 5:3), and the matter was settled when a search found Cyrus's decree (Ezra 6:1-12). The work of 1:14 was therefore the first stage: gathering wood and stone, clearing the site, and beginning to lay courses. Whether a foundation laid in 538 (Ezra 3:8-13) was still there in 520, or the first foundation was laid in 520, is debated; see the note at 2:18.

p: The work began on 21 September 520 BC by the usual conversion, 23 days after the first message.
b: The sixth month, twenty-fourth day, converts to 21 September 520 BC. The time between the message (29 August) and the start of work is 23 days (the 1st to the 24th of the month is a difference of 23). The book does not say what filled those days; cutting wood and gathering labor are likely. The Hebrew puts this date after the last sentence of chapter 1, and the Greek attaches it to the front of chapter 2 (see the note on the numbering in the book's introduction). Another "twenty-fourth" falls on the ninth month three months later (2:10, 18, 20), the day on which the blessing is promised.

t: Claude's theory: the date was chosen for the feast
p: Claude's reading: the message was timed for the Feast of Booths, the festival of Solomon's dedication.
b: Claude's theory, resting on 1 Kings 8:2, 65-66 and Ezra 3:1-6. The seventh month holds the autumn festivals, and the twenty-first day is the seventh day of Booths, with the solemn assembly on the eighth (Leviticus 23:34-36, 39-43). Solomon dedicated the first Temple at this feast (1 Kings 8:2). A prophet who wants a discouraged community to see the new house against the old would choose the one day of the year on which the whole people remembered the old dedication. The comparison "this house in its first glory" (2:3) then falls on listeners who have just been reading, or hearing, about it. This overlaps with commentators who point out that the date falls in the feast (for example Meyers and Meyers); that Haggai chose the date for this reason is my own inference, since the book does not say so.

a: on the twenty-first day of the month
p: 17 October 520 BC by the usual conversion, about four weeks after work began.
b: The seventh month, twenty-first day, converts to 17 October 520 BC. The work had begun four weeks earlier (1:15). By now the builders could see the size of the task, and the old people could compare it with what they remembered. Booths lasted seven days with a solemn assembly on the eighth (Leviticus 23:36); the twenty-first is the seventh and last of the booth days, and the eighth day (the 22nd) is the solemn assembly. Pilgrims from the countryside would be in Jerusalem, so this message reaches more of the people than the first one, which was addressed to the two leaders. The Septuagint puts the sixth-month date of 1:15 at the front of 2:1 as well (see the note on numbering).

t: The first house and the second
p: The old people had seen Solomon's Temple before 586 BC. Ezra records the old men's tears when a foundation was laid.
b: Solomon's Temple was burned in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:9), and 520 is 66 years later. Anyone who saw it in full splendor would be over 70. Ezra remembers exactly this: when the foundation was laid, many of the old priests and Levites and heads of families who had seen the first house wept aloud, while others shouted for joy (Ezra 3:12-13). Cyrus's decree names sixty cubits for both height and width (Ezra 6:3), and says nothing of Solomon's gold, bronze work or cedar. Zechariah, speaking in the same months, asks who dares despise "the day of small things" (Zechariah 4:10). Ezekiel 40-48 had described a still greater Temple that the builders did not follow.

a: Is it not like nothing in your eyes?
p: The LORD names the listeners' discouragement honestly: the question gives no false comfort.
b: The Hebrew ka'ayin is "like nothing" or "as nothing." The question is not rebuking the people but speaking for their feeling, and it expects the answer "yes." God does not say the house is splendid. He says "be strong" (2:4) and "I am with you." The shape of the speech is a pattern for encouragement: name the grief, then give the promise. The same question can be heard as the voice of the old men standing at the foundation. The contrast with the wealth of the nations (2:7-8) is deliberate.

p: The call is the one given to Joshua at the Jordan and to Solomon at the start of the first Temple.
b: "Be strong" is the encouragement given to Joshua before the conquest (Joshua 1:6-9) and to Solomon by David before the Temple was built: "Be strong, and get it done" (1 Chronicles 28:10). Haggai says it three times, to the governor, the high priest, and all the people, and each time with the same verb. The high priest has the same name as the first Joshua. The echo makes the rebuilding a new conquest and a new building commission at once. The promise attached to it, "I am with you," is the one in Joshua 1:9 too.

p: 'Am ha'arets means different groups in different books. In Haggai it most likely names the Judean community as a whole.
b: The site's Plain renders 'am ha'arets "the people of the land" in every book and notes that who is meant differs by passage. In earlier books it can be the landowning citizens of Judah (2 Kings 11:14, 18; 2 Kings 21:24) or, in Ezra, the non-exiled neighbors who opposed the Temple (Ezra 4:4). Haggai uses it for those he calls on to work with Zerubbabel and Joshua, so it is positive here. Most commentators take it as the ordinary Judeans, the whole population including the returnees (Meyers and Meyers, Petersen); a few think of the long-resident landowners, and a smaller group has "the people of the land" as a class that held legal rights. The text names no further group.

a: my spirit is standing among you
t: The spirit at the Exodus and now
p: God's spirit "standing" among them recalls the pillar and the tent at the Exodus.
b: The verb "standing" ('omedet) is used of the cloud pillar standing between Egypt and Israel (Exodus 14:19) and of the LORD's presence going with Israel (Exodus 33:14-16). Isaiah 63:11-14 remembers "the one who put his holy spirit within them" at the Exodus. Haggai says that spirit has not left the people. The promise is not magic: it stands beside the command "work" (2:4) and "do not be afraid." Zechariah's famous line, "not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit" (Zechariah 4:6), is addressed to Zerubbabel in the same year. On the later Jewish teaching that the Holy Spirit was gone from the Second Temple, see the variant at 1:8.

a: I am about to shake the heavens and the earth
p: Hebrews quotes this verse in the Greek form and reads the "shaking" as the removal of what can be shaken.
b: The shaking of heaven and earth is the language of the LORD's appearing: at Sinai the mountain trembled (Exodus 19:18; Judges 5:4-5), and on the day of the LORD the heavens quake (Isaiah 13:13; Joel 3:16). In Hebrews 12:26-27 the writer quotes the promise "Once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heaven," taking over the Septuagint's "once more" (eti hapax) and rewording the rest, and explains that "once more" points to the removal of created things that can be shaken, so that what cannot be shaken remains. The Hebrew in Haggai lists four things (heavens, earth, sea, dry ground) and the writer of Hebrews shortens it to two. Haggai's own hearers heard political upheaval (see the next note); the author of Hebrews hears the end of the age.

a: Once more, in a little while
p: The "little while" was read as the Persian upheavals of 521-520, the fall of Persia, Rome, or the end of the age.
b: The Hebrew 'od achat me'at hi' is "yet once, it is a little (while)." Readings: (1) The political turmoil of Darius's accession and the revolts that followed (522-520) were the first tremors, and Haggai expects more (Meyers and Meyers, Petersen, Kessler). (2) A later upheaval such as the fall of the Persian Empire to Alexander in 330 BC, which readers who look for a date in history have suggested. (3) The Hellenistic or Roman world, or the coming of Christ (many Christian writers). (4) The end of the age, as Hebrews 12:26-27 hears it, which stretches "a little while" across centuries. Prophets often use "soon" without a date (the topic soon); the verse itself fixes no year.

p: Chemdat kol-haggoyim has been read as the nations' treasures, as Christ, and as the believers from the nations.
b: Chemdah is "desire" or "what is desired," and the noun chemdat is singular, but the verb "will come" (uva'u) is plural. That mismatch is the problem. The simplest reading of the grammar is a collective: the desirable things of all the nations will come. The next verse, "The silver belongs to me, and the gold" (2:8), supports it, because the nations' wealth is what flows to Jerusalem in Isaiah 60:5-11 and Isaiah 61:6. Radak (David Kimhi) on 2:7 explains that God will move the nations to bring silver, gold and other precious goods to the Temple, so he reads the "desire" as the nations' valuables. The Targum Jonathan keeps the same singular noun and the plural verb ("they will come, the desire of all the peoples"), so it does not settle the grammar. I found no Rashi comment on this verse, and I did not check whether any Hebrew manuscript has a plural noun. The Latin Vulgate has "the Desired of all nations will come" (veniet desideratus cunctis gentibus), and the church read that as a title of Christ; the Septuagint has "the chosen things of all the nations will come." See the variant, and the "Where Christians differ" card on this chapter. The Plain follows the Hebrew with "prized things."

p: The language is the dedication of the tabernacle and of Solomon's Temple, and Ezekiel's vision of the glory returning.
b: The verb "fill" with kavod, "glory," is the verb of Sinai and the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34-35) and of the dedication of Solomon's house, when the cloud filled it and the priests could not stand to minister (1 Kings 8:10-11). Ezekiel saw the glory leave the first Temple (Ezekiel 10:18-19) and promised that it would return to a rebuilt house (Ezekiel 43:1-5). Haggai promises it to the house they are building. Whether that glory means a visible presence, the wealth of the nations (2:8), or the worship of the Gentiles is part of the discussion in the next notes. Jewish tradition holds that the Shekhinah did not fill the Second Temple (Bavli Yoma 21b, see the variant at 1:8).

a: The silver belongs to me, and the gold belongs to me
p: The LORD owns the silver and gold. The Temple will be furnished, as in Solomon's day, from what is already his.
b: Psalm 50:10 has the same ownership claim about the cattle on a thousand hills, and David's prayer at the first Temple gift says "everything in the heavens and on the earth is yours" (1 Chronicles 29:11). In 520 the Judeans were poor, and the decree of Cyrus meant that at least part of the cost came from the royal treasury (Ezra 6:4, 8). Haggai points the other way: the money that should come is not the community's but the LORD's, and he is able to move it. The thought is not a promise of wealth to every builder. It is an answer to 2:3: the house looks like nothing because the means of splendor have not yet been given.

a: The last glory of this house will be greater than the first
p: Jews and Christians have answered this promise differently. Whether "last" means the house or the glory is also open.
b: The Hebrew is ambiguous: "the glory of this house, the last, more than the first" can mean the later glory of the house (as the Plain reads it) or the later house (this one) being greater than the former (Solomon's). Answers: (1) Jewish: Rashi on 2:9 reports that Rav and Samuel disagreed about what "greater" refers to, one saying "in the building" and the other "in the years" (410 years for the first house and 420 for the second, in Rashi's figures). I have not checked which sage held which view or where in the Talmud the discussion stands. Those who say "building" can point to Herod's rebuilding of the Temple from about 20 BC, which Josephus describes at length (Antiquities 15.11); that link is my inference, not Rashi's. Separately, the Talmud lists the Shekhinah among five things the Second Temple lacked (Yoma 21b). (2) Christian: Christ's presence in the Temple, from Simeon's arms to the money changers' tables (Luke 2:27-32; John 2:19-21), or the church as God's true temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:20-22; 1 Peter 2:5). (3) Future: a still-future temple filled with glory (Dispensationalist readings, with Ezekiel 40-48). (4) Critical: a hope the community held and the book offers as an encouragement, not a prediction of measurable events.
r: Luke 2:27-32; John 2:19-21; 1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:20-22; 1 Peter 2:5; Ezekiel 43:1-5

a: On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month
p: This is the date of the priests' ruling, of the promise "from this day," and of the second message to Zerubbabel.
b: The ninth month (Kislev), twenty-fourth day, converts to 18 December 520 BC. It falls in the rainy season, when winter grain is sown, and about three months after the work began (1:15). Three messages carry this date: the priests' ruling (2:10-14), the turn to blessing (2:15-19), and the word to Zerubbabel (2:20-23); the book says "a second time" at 2:20 for the last. Zechariah's first message came a month earlier, in the eighth month (Zechariah 1:1), and his night visions two months later, in the eleventh (Zechariah 1:7).

p: Torah here is a priest's ruling on a case. The Plain notes the sense each time.
b: Torah is "teaching" or "instruction," and the Plain's "law" has to be read with that in mind. In the earlier writings the priests gave torah, a ruling on what is holy, clean or unclean (Leviticus 10:10-11; Deuteronomy 17:8-11; Jeremiah 18:18; Ezekiel 44:23). Haggai asks them a question that they alone can answer. Malachi says the priest's lips should guard knowledge, for people seek torah from his mouth (Malachi 2:7). So the prophet does what the law told the people to do: he goes to the priests, not to a prophetic vision, for the answer, and then draws his own conclusion from it.

p: Meat from an offering is holy, but touching it with a robe's fold does not make other food holy.
b: "Holy meat" (besar-qodesh) is meat from an offering that only priests and their households may eat. Leviticus says that whatever touches the meat of a sin offering becomes holy (Leviticus 6:27, English numbering; Hebrew 6:20). The priests' answer shows that holiness passes by direct touch only: if the meat's holiness is carried in a fold of a robe, a second item that touches the fold does not become holy. The question lists bread, stew, wine and oil, the ordinary food of a household and of the Temple's offerings. The tension with Leviticus 6:27 is open. That verse says whatever touches the flesh of the sin offering becomes holy. One natural reading is that the law speaks of direct contact with the flesh itself, while Haggai asks about a second step (a garment, then food); whether the priests rely on a rule beyond what Leviticus records is not settled here. Holiness is real but limited; it is not catching. The answer is "no," given in one word.

a: made unclean by a dead person
p: Corpse uncleanness is the strongest in the law, and it spreads by touch. The priests say yes.
b: "Unclean by a dead person" (teme' nefesh) is the uncleanness of touching a corpse, which lasted seven days and could be removed only with the water of impurity, sprinkled on the third and seventh days (Numbers 19:11-13). A person made unclean in this way makes what he touches unclean (Numbers 19:22), and a priest was forbidden to eat holy gifts until he was clean (Leviticus 22:4-7). So the priests' second answer is that uncleanness spreads where holiness does not. The two answers set up the lesson of 2:14: a community that touches the holy without building the Temple does not make its works holy; its uncleanness taints all it handles.

a: So it is with this people, and so with this nation
p: The text does not say. Commentators suggest the Judean community, the Samaritans of Ezra 4, or the whole land.
b: The Plain does not pick a referent the Hebrew does not name. Views: (1) The Judean community itself, whose worship at the altar (Ezra 3:3-6) is unclean as long as the Temple is unbuilt (Ackroyd, Meyers and Meyers, Petersen, Kessler; the most common view). (2) The Samaritans of Ezra 4:1-5, who offered to help and were refused: Rothstein argued in 1908 that Haggai speaks of them. Most scholars reject this because the phrase "this people" is Haggai's own for the Judeans (1:2) and because the word "nation" (goy) is also used loosely. (3) The people of the land who did not go into exile, whose offerings were thought corrupt. (4) The whole land, in a general judgment that the unbuilt Temple has tainted everything. Haggai is the speaker, and the hearers are the same group he began with.

p: "From this day and up" can look ahead or behind. The next phrase, "before a stone was laid," decides for looking back.
b: The Hebrew min hayyom hazzeh vamma'lah is "from this day and upward." Elsewhere the same phrase means "onward" (1 Samuel 16:13), and many translations read "from this day on." Here the next words, mittérem sum even 'el-even, "before a stone was put on a stone," show that the speaker is looking back from today to the time before building started, so the Plain reads "on back." The Greek has hyperano, "above," at 2:15 and epekeina, "beyond," at 2:18, and the same "before" at 2:15. The Plain keeps one meaning in both places, 2:15 and 2:18. The sense is the same: put the years before the work beside the years after.

a: a stone was laid on a stone
p: The phrase marks the time before the courses of the new walls were laid. Whether a foundation already stood is debated (see 2:18).
b: "Stone on stone" (even 'el-even) names the work of setting courses. The Temple's wall was built of large dressed stones, each laid upon the other (Ezra 5:8). It looks back to the time before the courses were laid, which fits either view of the foundation: the building of the walls had not begun, whether or not a foundation from 538 stood. Whether a foundation laid in 538 (Ezra 3:8-13) was still there in 520, or the first foundation was laid in 520, is debated; see the note at 2:18. The word for temple is hekhal, "great hall," the same as Ezra 3:6, which the Plain renders "temple" in both places. Whether this refers to the whole building or to its sanctuary hall is not clear.

p: The Hebrew gives numbers without units. The Greek adds "seahs" and "measures" (sata, metretai).
b: The Hebrew has "twenty" for the heap and "fifty" for the vat; the unit is left out, and the Greek supplies barley in sata (dry measures) for the heap and metretai (liquid measures) for the vat. The Hebrew word at the vat is purah, which is a "winepress" in Isaiah 63:3 and seems here to name the measure drawn from it. The point is the ratio: half the grain (ten for twenty) and two fifths of the wine (twenty for fifty). The Plain says "heap that should have held twenty measures" to make it clear that the number is the expected yield. "In those days" is literally "from their being" (mehiyotam), an unclear phrase meaning "since they were" or "how they were."

t: The old plagues of the land
p: Blight and mildew are the covenant curse of Deuteronomy 28; hail is the plague of Exodus 9.
b: "Blight" (shiddafon) is a scorching wind that withers grain, and "mildew" (yeraqon) is a yellow or green discoloration of leaf and ear. Deuteronomy 28:22 lists them together in the curses ("with blight and mildew"), Solomon's prayer names them (1 Kings 8:37), and Amos 4:9 says "I struck you with blight and mildew," the very wording Haggai repeats. Hail is the seventh plague of Egypt (Exodus 9:22-26). Haggai's three plagues are therefore the old curses that fell on a people who had not yet returned to the LORD, and Amos 4:9 is the closest parallel.

a: from the day the LORD's temple was founded
p: Does "the day the temple was founded" mean this 24th of Kislev, the earlier foundation in Ezra 3, or the day in Cyrus's reign?
b: The Hebrew verb yussad ("was founded") can describe a past event, a present ceremony, or an ongoing process. This is the one statement of the question for the book: Whether a foundation laid in 538 (Ezra 3:8-13) was still there in 520, or the first foundation was laid in 520, is debated; see the note at 2:18. Views: (1) The 24th of the ninth month, 520, is the day of a ceremony (a refounding or foundation-laying rite) with sacrifices; this fits "from the twenty-fourth day... from the day" as a restatement (Ackroyd, Petersen, Meyers and Meyers; Bedford argues that little or nothing was built before 520, a minority view). (2) The reference is to the earlier foundation of Ezra 3:8-13 in Cyrus's second year, and the new work resumes from it. (3) Zechariah 4:9 says Zerubbabel's hands laid this house's foundation and will finish it, which Ezra 5:16 assigns to Sheshbazzar; the sources do not agree on who laid the first foundation or when. All three views are debated. The Plain keeps the two phrases side by side and does not decide.

a: Even the vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate and the olive tree
p: The vine, fig, pomegranate and olive belong to the praise of the promised land.
b: The vine, fig, pomegranate and olive appear in the list of the land's gifts in Deuteronomy 8:8 and in the spies' report (Numbers 13:23). Joel 1:12 lists the vine, the fig and the pomegranate among the trees that wither in a drought. In December the vine, fig and pomegranate stand bare, and the olive, which is evergreen, is harvested in autumn and early winter, so its harvest was still due or failing; "have not borne fruit" means "have not borne this year," not that they never bear. The promise of blessing is given when no harvest has yet come; the people must believe it on the word of the LORD, and the next summer's figs and olives will show whether it is true. The four trees are the opposite of the empty barn.

a: From this day on I will bless you
p: The blessing starts before any crop comes. Zechariah 8:9-12, from the same years, says the same.
b: The pivot of the book is "from this day on I will bless." It reverses the curses of 1:6-11 and 2:16-17. The blessing is promised on the day of the decision, and the proof comes later. Zechariah 8:9-12 says that before the foundation was laid there was no wage for people or animals, but now the LORD will sow peace, the vine will give fruit, the ground its produce and the heavens their dew. Malachi 3:10-12 uses the same images for the storehouse. The promise does not guarantee wealth to everyone who builds a church; it is addressed to this people at this point in the covenant story (see the note at 1:9). Ezra 6:14 says the elders "went on building and doing well" as the prophets spoke.

a: on the twenty-fourth day of the month
p: The second message to Zerubbabel comes on the same day as the priests' ruling and the turn to blessing.
b: The 24th of the ninth month, 18 December 520 BC, carries all of 2:10-23. The book separates them by saying "a second time" and by changing the audience: the priests and the people in 2:10-19, Zerubbabel alone in 2:20-23. Some commentators think the two messages are one day's speech in two scenes; others, a later editor's arrangement of two separate days, since "a second time" would otherwise be unnecessary. The Plain keeps the book's text as it stands.

a: I am about to shake the heavens and the earth
p: This is the first half of 2:6 without the sea and dry land, and it is told to Zerubbabel alone.
b: The line repeats 2:6, minus the sea and dry ground, and the next verse shows its target: the thrones and armies of the nations. It is the pair of the Temple oracle (2:6-9): the first shaking brings the nations' wealth to the house; the second overthrows their power. Both are given no date. A "Still to come" reading takes them as the end of the age (Hebrews 12:26-27 is the New Testament use); a historical reading takes them as a hope for a political change in the Persian world, tied to the unsettled years after Darius took the throne; a critical reading sees it as a hope the book records, with no later fulfillment.

p: Hafakh is the verb of Sodom's destruction, and of Nineveh's announced fate in Jonah.
b: Hafakh, "overturn," is used of the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:25, 29) and Amos 4:11 compares an overturning in Israel to Sodom's. Jonah calls out that Nineveh "will be overturned" (Jonah 3:4), a verb that can also mean "turn around," which is how Jonah's story ends. The verb here is used of a throne and of a chariot, the signs of royal rule and military power. A chariot overturned is a war machine upended. The sound-picture is of a collapse, not a slow decline. The Hebrew has hafakhti twice (throne, chariot), and the Plain keeps "overturn" for both; the middle verb, hishmadti, is "wipe out."

a: each by the sword of his brother
p: The Holy War picture is Gideon's night battle and Ezekiel's Gog: God makes the enemy kill itself.
b: When Gideon's three hundred blew their horns, "the LORD turned each man's sword against his comrade" (Judges 7:22). Ezekiel's Gog falls the same way: "The sword of each man will be against his brother" (Ezekiel 38:21). Zechariah 14:13 has the same panic. The horses and riders recall Exodus 15:1, where "horse and rider" went down into the sea. Haggai's picture is not a human campaign led by Zerubbabel: God does the shaking and the people do not fight. It is Holy War in the old sense (the topic holy-war), where the victory is the LORD's. Rashi on 2:22 reads the verse as saying that the Persian kingdom, which then ruled the world, would fall into the hands of another kingdom.

p: Bayyom hahu' points to the day of the shaking, not to a date. It is not a fixed term for the end.
b: "On that day" is a link to what came before: the day the nations are overturned (2:22). In the prophets the phrase often belongs to the "day of the LORD" (the topic day-of-the-lord), but it is also used of an ordinary future moment. Haggai gives no date. The promise to Zerubbabel is therefore tied to the shaking, not to the Temple's completion. If the shaking is read as political upheaval in 520 BC, the "day" is near; if it is the end of the age, the promise waits for it, which is how Dispensationalist and many other Christian readings take it.

a: I will take you, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel
p: The book ends on a promise that the sources never say was kept, and Zerubbabel does not appear again.
b: Zerubbabel last appears in the sources in the work on the Temple. Ezra 6 does not name him at the dedication (Ezra 6:14-18), and no text says what became of him. Proposals: he finished his term and was succeeded by another governor; the Persians removed him as a suspected claimant to the throne (a guess found in older scholarship, with no source); he died; or the hope for a Davidic ruler was shifted to the high priest, as in Zechariah 6:9-14, where the crown ends on Joshua (the Hebrew of Zechariah 6:11 is debated). Sirach 49:11 compares Zerubbabel to a signet ring on the right hand, and Sirach 49:12 names Jeshua beside him as a builder of the Temple. In 1 Esdras 3-5 Zerubbabel is a bodyguard of Darius who wins a contest and leads the return.
r: Ezra 6:14-18; Zechariah 6:9-14; Sirach 49:11-12; 1 Esdras 3:1-5:6; Matthew 1:12-13; Luke 3:27

p: Both words are David's. Zerubbabel is addressed in the language of the Davidic king.
b: "My servant" ('avdi) and "I have chosen" (bachar) are the LORD's words for David (1 Kings 11:34; Psalm 78:70). Servant is also Moses' title, Israel's in Isaiah 41:8 and the prophet's in Isaiah 42:1. Zechariah, in the same years, calls the coming one "my servant the Branch" (Zechariah 3:8). Haggai does not call Zerubbabel "king" or "anointed." He says "servant" and "chosen." The silence is part of the puzzle: a Persian governor could not be called king, and the book is careful. The words nevertheless tie the grandson of Jehoiachin back to David.

t: A seal ring, and the curse reversed
p: Jeremiah 22:24-25 says the LORD would tear Jehoiachin off like a seal ring. Haggai says Jehoiachin's grandson will be one.
b: A seal ring (chotam) carried the owner's mark and stamped his authority on a document; losing it was losing power (Genesis 38:18; Esther 3:10). Jeremiah 22:24 says that if Coniah (Jehoiachin) were the seal ring on the LORD's right hand, he would be pulled off. Haggai names the grandson and reverses the image: God will make him the seal ring. The word is chosen for its fit with the Davidic line. "Seal ring" is the site's wording in Jeremiah; the English "signet ring" is common. Sirach 49:11 uses the signet image of Zerubbabel; Sirach 49:12 names Jeshua son of Jozadak as a builder beside him. Rashi on 2:23 sets Zerubbabel against his grandfather Jeconiah, who was decreed childless: Jeconiah's repentance availed, Zerubbabel was born to him, and he was made as a signet. The promise cannot be read as ruling power in Haggai's day, and the book gives no sign that it was kept; Christian, Jewish and critical readings differ (see the card).
r: Jeremiah 22:24-25; Genesis 38:18; Song of Songs 8:6; Esther 3:10; Sirach 49:11-12
